opener.heading: Week 28: Beach & Water Fun 🏖️
about: Water is the material all week. Azlyn floats things and sinks them, moves a bucket of it across the yard by sponge, sends it down five bottle chutes taped to the fence, and paints a wall the sun wipes clean behind her. The same question comes back in a new form every day: what does water do, and what makes it stay where you put it? By Thursday she has a fleet of boats, a sea sealed in a bottle, four name stones and a beach she built in the yard.

No holiday lands this week, so the heat is the thing to plan around. Monday is the longest stretch outdoors of the seven days and wants shade, a hat and a drink she can reach without asking. Saturday's sand goes under a trash bag and comes back out on Wednesday, Friday's boats sail again in the paddling pool on Thursday, and the salt water on Tuesday takes half an hour in the sun to show what it did. Nothing she makes gets thrown out before the week is finished.
azlyn: Shape decides what floats. One square of foil sinks as a ball and carries a cargo of pasta as a boat.
Water is what makes sand hold. Dry sand slumps out of the cup, damp sand keeps its corners, and one pitcher too many turns the lot to soup.
The long out-breath, down a straw, under a feather, and up at a paper spiral that only turns for a slow one.
Pouring, aiming and squeezing with pitchers, sponges, a squeezy bottle and chutes she moves herself until the water lands where she wants it.
That she can finish a job she can see. Grubby pile on her left, clean row on her right, and she works from one side to the other.
you: Same material, different shape, opposite result
Open-ended materials outperform toys, and cheap ones outperform expensive ones
Slow exhalation is the body's own calming switch
Give three tools and let her choose
Visible results are what sustain a child's effort
Competition at three works when everyone wins something real
Historical injustice, explained plainly, does not damage a three-year-old
shopping: A bag of play sand (substitute: dry garden soil, or rice for the dry half)
Clear plastic bottles, 500 ml, 3, labels peeled off
Plastic bottles in mixed sizes, 5, for the water wall
A paddling pool (substitute: 2 large storage boxes, or the bath)
A paper grocery bag, for Thursday's beachcombing
An empty margarine or ice cream tub
An ice cube tray, for molding sand
A funnel (substitute: the top third of a spare bottle, cut off)
Dried pasta, a handful, or 20 coins
A craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
Plain paper, 8 sheets, for tickets, sails, flags, the sign and the spinner
Dark paper, 2 sheets (substitute: brown parcel paper, or a flattened cereal box colored dark)
Tissue paper or paper towels, 3 sheets
A ping-pong ball (substitute: a scrunched foil ball)
A feather (substitute: a torn strip of tissue)
Brushes: 1 wide decorating brush, 1 paintbrush, 1 old toothbrush, 1 nail brush, 1 dustpan brush
Spoons, 4, one metal and one a teaspoon
Old towels, 5, and every towel in the house on Thursday
A laundry basket and one smaller basket
A bag, a towel and a book to pack for the train
A phone, for the timer and the photographs
A cloth for drying the stones
A fence, shed side or wall (substitute: a large flattened box propped against a wall)
Eight small kitchen things that can get wet: 2 corks, 2 jar lids, a peg, a bottle cap, plus a spoon and a craft stick from elsewhere on this list
The grubby outdoor toys: the trike, the rain boots, the plastic animals, the doll from under the hedge
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs, and carries things while he moves, which in a week of water means he carries it. He gets his own cup, his own sponge and his own end of the towel every day, and he stays within arm's reach of anything full.

days.title: Float It or Sink It
days.prepTonight: Stand the dishpan on two old dish towels by the back door with the foil and the marker. Buy a bag of play sand today; tomorrow runs on it.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Float Pile and the Sink Pile

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Bowl of Corks and Lids

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath With the Fleet In It

opening.title: The Float Pile and the Sink Pile
opening.need: 1 dishpan half filled with water · 8 small things from the kitchen · 1 dish towel.
steps: Let her pick them: a spoon, a cork, a lid, a peg, a craft stick, a bottle cap. Nothing that matters if it gets wet.
One at a time, and she calls it before she drops it. Sinkers on the dish towel, floaters beside it.
Ask what the floating pile has in common. Take the answer as it arrives and leave it until 9:15.

main.title: Ball, Boat, Same Foil
materials: Dried pasta, a handful, or 20 coins as cargo
Paper and a pen for her guesses
1 plastic cup and 1 shallow tray for Kreston
steps: Tear two squares of foil the same size, a hand span each, and lay one on the other so she sees they match.
Scrunch the first into a tight ball. Press the second over your fist and pinch the sides up into a boat.
Write her guesses on the paper before either touches the water: ball, floats or sinks; boat, floats or sinks.
Spread the dish towels, stand the bowl on them, fill two-thirds and mark the water level with the marker. Both shapes go in at once, one in each hand.
Give the boat a cargo: five pieces of pasta, one at a time. It sits lower in the water and stays up, while the ball lies on the bottom carrying nothing.
Now she builds the boat and you do nothing. Hers comes out a different shape, floats anyway, and the result goes on the paper under yours.
main.tip: Drop them together rather than one after the other. She will ask you to flatten the ball out and try again.

outside.title: Leaf Boats Down the Gutter
paras: Take a two-liter bottle of water to the top of a driveway or a dead-end stretch, well back from any through road; July gutters are bone dry. Pour a slow stream into the curb channel and send leaves down it, one each. They snag on grit and stop dead, and she kneels on the sidewalk side to clear the channel with her fingers. Save the last of the bottle for the drink she forgets to ask for.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks. Give him his own cup and a shallow tray with a finger of water in it at the far end of the towels. He fills the cup, walks three steps, tips it and goes back for more. He runs that loop for five minutes, wanders off, and comes back to it across the morning.

second.title: Four Boats and a Wave
second.intro: The bowl stays where it is and the fleet gets bigger: four boats out of the recycling.
materials: 1 empty margarine or ice cream tub
The bowl of water from this morning
steps: Four piles along the table: foil, the margarine tub, the caps, the sticks. She builds one boat from each and you keep your hands off three.
Foil goes over your fist again. The margarine tub is a boat already. Five craft sticks tape side by side into a raft, the sixth upright in the middle.
The six caps tape rim to rim into a block, two rows of three.
Tear four rough sails. Tape a straw mast into the foil boat and another into the tub, a sail to each. The raft's sail goes on its standing stick; the cap boat's folds into an L and tapes flat.
Float all four at once and ask which boat the wave will beat.
One hand each side of the bowl, rock it once. That is the wave. Watch what tips, then rock harder.
Keep going until one boat is left upright. Mend the sunk ones and sail again.
second.tip: Hand her the bowl for the last few waves and let her decide how hard.

alternatives: One boat each, no sails, straight into the bath.
Race two boats across the bowl by blowing through the straws.
Sort the recycling into things that would float and things that would not.
outAgain: Playgroup, and the paddling trays will be out in this heat
A friend's garden, if anyone has a hose and the patience
The splash pad, early enough for a shaded bench
The park at the end of the day, once the grass is back in shade

aroundWorld.title: Australia: Swim Between the Flags 🏖️
paras: Australian beaches carry two flags in the sand, a red and yellow pair at each end of a stretch of water. The water between them is the part the lifesavers are watching, and children there learn the phrase before they can swim. The flags move up and down the beach as the currents shift, so the safe patch is never in the same place twice.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Push two red and yellow paper flags into the grass and let Azlyn set the safe water. Eat fairy bread between them: white bread, butter and a heavy shake of sprinkles, cut into triangles.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Surf Life Saving Australia has over 180,000 members, and most of the people on patrol are volunteers.

days.krestonPM: At 13 months he climbs, and a dishpan on the floor is a thing to climb into. Sit him beside it with the margarine tub boat, mast pulled out, the one thing in the fleet too big to go in his mouth. He bangs the surface flat-handed to make his own wave.

insight.headline: Same material, different shape, opposite result.
paras: Two identical squares of foil went into the same water and did opposite things. Azlyn cannot hold the density explanation at three and she does not need it. She keeps the rule underneath: the same stuff arranged two ways behaves two ways. Children this age work out physical rules by watching one thing change while everything else stays still, and you set that up for her by tearing the squares the same size. She will ask why the boat floats. Answer with another test. Flatten the ball out, fold it into a third shape and put it back in the water.

days.safety: Standing water. Kreston is 13 months, he walks, and he can drown in the depth of a dishpan in silence. He stays within arm's reach whenever it is full, and the bowl gets tipped the moment they stop. Torn foil scraps, pasta, corks, lids and bottle caps all go straight in his mouth, so keep the offcuts on the table and sweep before you put him down. The gutter run puts her hands at the edge of a live road, so stay between her and the road, and Kreston rides in the stroller with the brake on or holds your hand with the road on your side of him. July sun burns before it feels hot: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: Wet Sand Holds
days.prepTonight: Spread an old towel in the yard with the storage box and the bag of play sand on it. Rinse two clear 500 ml bottles and peel the labels for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Sand Tray on a Towel

opening.title: Raiding the Kitchen Drawer
opening.need: the kitchen drawer · 1 basket · the towel in the yard.
steps: Hand her the basket and two rules: nothing sharp, nothing that plugs in.
She chooses six things she thinks could shape sand. Let the daft ones through; a potato masher beats anything sold as a sand tool.
Lay them along the edge of the towel in the order she picked them. Ask which will hold a shape and let the guess sit until 9:15.

main.title: Wet Sand, Dry Sand
materials: 1 bag play sand (substitute: dry garden soil, or a bag of rice for the dry half only)
1 metal spoon, 1 sieve, 2 cups, 1 ice cube tray, 1 potato masher
steps: Box on the towel, dry sand two hands deep, tools along the edge.
Dry first. She fills both cups and the ice cube tray, turns them out and watches it slump. Sieve it, spoon it, pile it up.
Half a pitcher of water into one end. Mix it with the spoon and let her get her hands in. Fill a cup and turn it out; somewhere in that pitcher the sand starts holding.
Press a flat patch with the potato masher and let her stamp a print in it. Fill the ice cube tray and turn out blocks that keep their corners.
The rest of the pitcher goes in until it turns to soup. Ask her where it went wrong; dry sand from the far end is the repair.
Sweep the spills back into the box with the dustpan brush.
main.tip: Let her ruin it in step five. She has to see the soup to know that wet has two ends.

outside.title: Barefoot on Four Grounds
paras: Shoes off in the yard and walk four surfaces in a row: grass, paving, gravel or bark, and the doormat. Test the paving with your own hand first, because a July slab in full sun will burn her feet. Name each one as she stands on it and ask which she would sleep on.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and he will eat a handful of sand before you finish turning round, so he gets his own end of the towel and his own cup with a splash of water in it. Barefoot on grass is worth five minutes on its own at his age. He stands still and looks down at his feet.

second.title: The Train to the Seaside
second.intro: Four dining chairs in a line down the hall, and the 2:30 train is a real one.
materials: Paper for tickets and a sign, 2 sheets
1 hole punch, or 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only)
1 bag, 1 towel and 1 book to pack
steps: Chairs in a line, two and two, all facing the same way. The front one is the driver's and she picks who sits there.
Fold a sheet of paper into six, write SEASIDE on each panel with the marker and tear them apart into tickets.
She punches a hole in every ticket, or you snip a corner off each with the adult scissors.
The second sheet is the destination sign. She tells you the word, you write it, and it tapes to the front chair.
Pack the bag together: the towel, the book, and whatever else she says a person needs at the sea.
Everyone boards and hands over a ticket. Bang the saucepan lid for the whistle and pull out.
She calls the stops, you say what goes past the window, and the last stop is the sea.
second.tip: Keep two tickets back for the real train at 2:30. She hands one to an actual guard.

alternatives: One row of chairs, no tickets, straight to the sea.
Draw the view out of the window on the back of the sign.
Line the chairs up as a bus and go somewhere she names.
outAgain: A train ride, two stops out and two back, with her ticket in her hand
The station itself, if the timetable is against you, to watch them arrive
A bus ride instead, in the front seats right behind the driver
A shaded walk somewhere with water at the end of it
days.krestonPM: He rides too. At 13 months a moving train is hard work, all vibration and strangers and things sliding past the window, so a short hop out and back is plenty. Sit him on your lap facing the glass and name three things as they go.

insight.headline: Open-ended materials outperform toys, and cheap ones outperform expensive ones.
paras: A bag of play sand costs less than takeout and held her for twenty minutes at a stretch, three separate times before lunch. Sand has no finished state, so nothing she does to it counts as wrong, and she will take risks with it she would never take with a puzzle that has one right answer. She wrecked the wet sand on purpose to find where the edge was. Researchers who time children's play find the longest stretches over materials with no built-in outcome: sand, water, dough, blocks. The toy with a button and a song does one thing well, and she has finished it by Tuesday. Buy the sand.

days.safety: Sand in eyes, and sand in Kreston's mouth. Play sand only, never builder's sand, and keep it damp so it cannot blow about. The box stays at her end of the towel and he stays at the other end with his own cup. If it gets in her eyes, rinse with clean water and no rubbing. Four surfaces in the open take her out of the shade, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Slow Wave
days.prepTonight: The bottles are rinsed and the labels are off, so stand them on the counter with the cooking oil, the blue food coloring and the packing tape.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Lying on the Towel Looking Up

opening.title: Choosing the Blue
opening.need: 3 clear glasses of water · blue food coloring · 1 teaspoon · a bright window.
steps: One drop of coloring in the first glass, three in the second, six in the third. She counts them in and stirs each with the teaspoon.
Hold all three against the window: a swimming pool, the sea on a good day, the sea in a storm.
She picks the one that goes in the bottle at 9:15. Leave that glass at the front of the counter.

main.title: The Sea in a Bottle
materials: 2 clear plastic bottles, 500 ml, labels peeled off
1 funnel (substitute: the top third of a third bottle, cut off)
1 roll packing tape for sealing the lid
steps: Fill each bottle a third of the way from the pitcher. Add the blue she chose, counting the drops out loud, then cap and shake until the color is even.
Funnel in the neck. Pour the oil in slow, half the bottle each, stopping a hand's width from the top.
Lid on tight, neck wiped dry, then two full turns of packing tape over the lid and down onto the shoulder. This lid does not come off again.
Lay it flat and lift one end, slow as you can. One wave travels the whole length and slows when you do.
Now let her shake it as hard as she likes. Everything breaks into beads. Set it down and wait two minutes for the layers to find each other again.
The second bottle is hers from the start, you holding the funnel and saying nothing.
main.tip: Check the tape before you hand it over, and again next week. A leaking bottle is a cupful of oil on the carpet.

outside.title: Lying on the Towel Looking Up
paras: Spread a towel in the deepest shade you can find at eleven and lie down on your backs. July skies are busy: swifts working high up, a plane trail going soft at the edges, one leaf turning over. Take her bottle out and lay it beside her so the sun comes through it.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and this bottle is built for him. Once the tape is on, let him have it on the grass. It is heavy enough to be interesting, it rolls, and the blue keeps moving after he has stopped. He will carry it around the yard and bring it back to Azlyn.

second.title: What One Breath Can Move
second.intro: A blowing station goes up on the kitchen table.
materials: 1 feather, or a torn strip of tissue
Tissue paper or paper towels, 3 sheets
1 ping-pong ball, or a scrunched foil ball
steps: Two lines of masking tape down the table a hand's width apart, three feet long. That is the track, with a strip across each end.
A cotton ball each at the start line, a straw each, and blow them down the track. Race three or four times and let her win some.
Swap in the ping-pong ball. Heavier, slower, and it wants a long steady blow rather than a hard puff.
The feather comes off the table. She keeps it up with her mouth alone and you count out loud until it lands.
Tear the tissue paper into squares. Hold one flat on the wall, blow at it and take your hand away. It hangs a second or two.
Cut a spiral out of the paper yourself, from the outside in. Tape a loop of masking tape to the middle and hang it from a shelf edge.
Blow up at the spiral. A hard puff swings it about. One long slow out-breath turns it round and round.
second.tip: Keep the spiral. Leave it hanging, and on the afternoons that fall apart at four o'clock, take her over and both of you blow.

alternatives: Cotton ball races on the floor with no track.
Blow bubbles in a glass of water through a straw.
Keep one feather in the air between the three of you.
outAgain: A playground you've never been to, chosen for shade over equipment
The one with the water feature, if the heat holds
A woodland path where the whole walk is under trees
The duck pond, late enough that the sun is off the water
days.krestonPM: Cotton balls and a 13-month-old do not mix, so he gets the sealed bottle and the far end of the room. At the playground he wants the steps rather than the slide, so let him have the ladder with your hands hovering.

insight.headline: Slow exhalation is the body's own calming switch.
paras: Azlyn spent the afternoon on a breathing exercise and nobody mentioned breathing. The out-breath is the half of the cycle that slows the heart. A long exhale raises vagal tone and takes her off the accelerator. The paper spiral turns for a long steady stream of air and swings about for a hard puff, so she had to slow down to make it go round. Telling a wound-up three-year-old to take a deep breath fails; she gulps the air in and holds it. Give her something to move with her mouth and the long breath arrives on its own: a straw, a feather, birthday candles, bubbles in a glass.

days.safety: Cotton balls, the ping-pong ball and loose straws all fit down Kreston's throat. Count them out and count them back in before he is on the floor, and keep the whole station at the far end of the table. Flat on a towel in the shade they both still burn, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Water on the Wall
days.prepTonight: Stand the bucket, the brush, the sponge, the squeezy bottle and the chalk by the back door. Pile every grubby outdoor toy into one heap for tomorrow.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Painting the Sun Takes Back

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Water Wall on the Fence

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Two Cups and a Bowl of Water

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Cool Bath and a Long Book

opening.title: Brush, Sponge, Squeezy Bottle
opening.need: 1 bucket half filled with water · 1 wide brush · 1 large sponge · 1 empty squeezy bottle · one dry paving slab.
steps: Bucket on the slab, three tools beside it, one instruction: put water on this square of ground.
She tries all three. The brush strokes, the sponge prints, the bottle squirts a line she can aim. Say nothing about which is best.
Ask which she wants for the fence at 9:15. She takes all three.

main.title: The Painting the Sun Takes Back
materials: 1 wide house-painting brush (substitute: a dish brush)
A fence or shed side, and one dry paving slab
1 small sponge and 1 plastic cup for Kreston
steps: Bucket at the foot of the fence in what shade there is, pitcher beside it.
Brush first. She paints a long stripe along the fence and the beginning has gone by the time she reaches the end.
Sponge next, pressed flat on the shed door in whole prints. Count how long each lasts; the ones in shade hold longer.
She lays a hand on the paving, you paint round it, then chalk the outline before it vanishes. The water goes, the chalk ghost stays.
Squeezy bottle, filled from the pitcher. Squirting a line high up the wall is the best thing all morning; give it twenty minutes.
Last one is a race. She paints a shape at one end of the fence and runs to the other end and back before it dries.
main.tip: Keep the bucket in shade and top it up from the pitcher. A trip indoors to the tap ends the whole thing.

outside.title: Hot Wall, Cool Wall
paras: Take her round the outside of the house with one hand out, touching as she goes. The sunny wall, the shaded wall, the paving, the grass, the car hood (your hand first, always). July gives the biggest spread of the year. Finish in the coolest spot she found and have the drink there.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and copies whatever Azlyn is holding, so give him his own small sponge and a cup with an inch of water. He paints the paving by dropping the sponge and picking it up. Check the ground with your hand before you set him down in bare feet.

second.title: The Water Wall on the Fence
second.intro: Five bottles get taped to the fence with a bucket at the bottom.
materials: 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
A fence, shed side or wall (substitute: a large flattened box propped against a wall)
steps: Cut the bottles into open chutes while she stands back: bottom off, one long side out, lid left on. Tape every cut rim twice round; the edges come out sharp.
Knife away on a shelf. She picks where the first chute goes and you tape it at her angle.
Pour a pitcher in the top. Flat chutes hold onto it, steep ones throw it clear over the next.
Let her move it. One chute, one change, one pitcher, and the answer arrives in four seconds.
Add the second and third chutes so the water lands in each in turn. Bucket at the bottom, bowl under the worst leak.
All five up. She pours the whole pitcher in and you watch how much arrives in the bucket.
Tip the bucket back into the pitcher and run it again. Leave the wall up.
second.tip: Use about twice as much tape as looks necessary. A chute that peels off mid-pour costs you ten minutes.

alternatives: Two chutes, one bucket, and stop there.
Float bottle caps down the run and see which make it.
Tape the chutes to the side of the bath and do it indoors.
outAgain: A green space with a ball, kept to the shaded half of the field
The park with the big trees, for a picnic tea underneath them
The riverside path, a few degrees cooler than the street
The playground after five, once the metal has come off the boil
days.krestonPM: He is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so the water wall hands him a real job: filling his cup at the bucket and delivering it to the top chute. It arrives half empty. Take it, pour it in and tell him what it did. Out with the ball he chases it and falls over it.

insight.headline: Give three tools and let her choose.
paras: Three is the number that works inside a single job. One tool at the fence is an instruction. Ten tools for one wall stall her, and she stands there holding nothing. Three lets her compare, pick and change her mind inside a minute, and the picking is the part that kept her at the fence past the twenty minutes you expected. Choice inside limits you set is the whole trick: you decided it was water on the wall, she decided it was the squeezy bottle. Researchers looking at autonomy find children given a real choice within a set task stay longer and argue less. Setting out three things instead of one costs you nothing.

days.safety: Heat. This is the longest stretch outdoors all week, so shade, a hat, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and a drink she can reach without asking. Cut bottle edges are sharp, so tape every rim before it goes on the fence and check them with your thumb. A full bucket in the sun is standing water with a 13-month-old beside it, so tip it the moment you finish. The knife and the scissors stay with you, on a shelf between cuts.

days.title: The Toy Wash
days.prepTonight: Stand the two dishpans by the back door with the brushes, string and pegs in one. Throw a trash bag over the sand box so it is still damp on Wednesday.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Dirty Pile by the Door

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Clean Animals in a Row

opening.title: The Dirty Pile by the Door
opening.need: the pile from last night · 1 old towel to lay it on · her.
steps: Walk the garden and add to the heap: the trike, the rain boots, the plastic animals, the doll that has lived under the hedge since June.
Lay it out on the towel in a line, grubbiest at one end. She sets the order.
Ask which will take the longest. Leave the line where it is; at 9:15 she works down it.

main.title: The Two-Bowl Car Wash
materials: Warm water and a squirt of dish soap
1 length of string and 6 pegs for the drying line
The trike, the rain boots, the plastic animals and the dolls from the pile
1 small bowl, 1 sponge and 1 plastic animal for Kreston
steps: Tie the string between the fence and a chair leg at her knee height, low enough that no loop reaches anybody's neck, and hang the clothespins along it. That is the drying line.
Bowl one gets warm water and a squirt of liquid, bowl two clean water for rinsing. Her dirty line on the left, an empty towel on her right.
Three brushes, one demonstration each and then hands off: toothbrush for wheels and joints, nail brush for rain boot soles, sponge for the big flat sides.
Wash, rinse, then peg or lay out. Doll clothes on the line, the trike and the rain boots on the towel to drip.
Halfway down the pile, look at bowl one. The water is gray. Tip it on the plants and mix a fresh one.
Stand back at the end and look left, then right. Nothing on her left, a full row on her right.
main.tip: She will wash the same wheel for eleven minutes. Leave her on it.

outside.title: Wet Wheel Tracks
paras: Take the clean trike and one bowl of water onto the driest paving you have. She rides the front wheel through the water and out across the slabs, printing tracks that last a minute in this heat. Ride a curve, then a straight line, then a circle, and compare the marks.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and copying chores is starting in earnest. Give him a small bowl with an inch of water, one sponge and one plastic animal, on the towel where you can see him. He washes it the way he has watched Azlyn wash hers: in and out forty times. Stay within arm's reach of every bowl.

second.title: Painting With Sea Water
second.intro: Six spoons of salt in a jar of warm water make a paint that shows nothing for half an hour.
materials: Dark paper, 2 sheets (substitute: brown parcel paper, or a flattened cereal box colored dark with a crayon)
steps: Six tablespoons of salt into the jar of warm water. She counts them in and tips each one.
Stir with the spoon until the salt stops disappearing. The last of it sits on the bottom; the water is full.
Brush loaded, she paints on the first sheet of dark paper. It looks like wet paper, so tell her the sun finishes it.
Flat on the sunny windowsill and leave it. Go and do something else for half an hour; standing over it makes the wait worse.
Come back. White lines have come up out of nowhere, following every stroke her brush made.
Second sheet, bigger and wetter: her name, a handprint, the sea. Back on the sill.
Hold the dry one to the light and let her rub a line with one finger. The crystals come off on her skin.
second.tip: Warm water takes about twice the salt that cold water will. Start the jar hotter rather than stirring more salt into cold.

alternatives: Paint the paving with the salt water and watch the white come up outside.
Rock salt in a saucer of water on the sill, left for two days.
Draw with a white crayon and paint over it.
outAgain: Swimming, and the coolest hour of her day
The outdoor pool if yours has one open for the summer
The splash pad, if the pool line is round the block
Indoor playground with the air conditioning, when nobody can face a changing room
days.krestonPM: He goes in too. At 13 months he walks on land, and the pool floor is all drag and no grip, so both your hands stay on him. Twenty-five minutes, out while he is enjoying it, food within the half hour. Let Azlyn show him how to slap the surface.

insight.headline: Visible results are what sustain a child's effort.
paras: The grubby pile on her left shrank and the clean row on her right grew, and she could check her own progress without asking you. A three-year-old cannot hold an abstract goal for forty minutes, and she does not have to when the evidence sits in front of her in two lines. Effort follows visible change at this age, which is the reason she abandons tidying her bedroom: a room halfway through looks the same as a room she has not started. Set a job up so the work leaves a mark she can see. Clipping washing, filling a jar, laying the table.

days.safety: Two full bowls at Kreston's exact height, and he walks now. Mix the water warm rather than hot, keep the soapy bowl at the back out of his reach, and tip both the moment she finishes. Soap in the eyes ends the morning, so the rinse bowl stays clean. Run the drying line at knee height and never at her chest, because a line at her chest is at Kreston's neck, and take it down once the last thing is dry. The wash runs on open paving: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Beach Games in the Garden
days.prepTonight: Put the buckets, the sponges and the chalk out by the back step. Drag the paddling pool out of the shed and hose it down; Thursday stands or falls on it.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Chalk Sea You Jump Into

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Best Castle, Best Door, Best Moat

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Feet in a Bowl, Book on Her Knees

opening.title: A Stone for Every Player
opening.need: 4 flat stones · 1 bowl of water and a cloth · 1 permanent marker.
steps: Hunt four flat stones from the yard or the pot plants, one for every person in the house. She chooses whose is whose.
Wash them in the bowl and dry them on the cloth. Wet stones will not take a marker.
Write the four names on with the marker while she tells you which is which. They mark the buckets at 9:15 and the castles at 1:00.

main.title: Moving the Sea by Sponge
materials: 1 shallow tray for Kreston, an inch of water in it
1 stick of chalk for the lines
steps: Chalk a start line and a finish line as far apart as the garden allows. Grass between them if you have it.
Two buckets on the start line, filled from the pitcher and from the tap. Two empty ones on the finish line, a name stone in front of each.
A sponge each, and one rule that never bends: nobody may carry a bucket.
Two minutes on the phone timer. Soak, run, squeeze, run back. Towel on the finish line for wet feet.
Stop dead on the timer and look. Tip the first finish bucket into the pitcher, mark the level with your thumb, empty it, then do the second and see whose comes higher.
Round two, and she changes one thing: two sponges at once, a bigger sponge, a longer timer, both hands.
main.tip: Play it for real. Run, drop things, lose. A three-year-old spots a grown-up going easy on her from a long way off.

outside.title: The Chalk Sea You Jump Into
paras: Chalk a wide wavy sea across the paving with three or four islands in it, big enough to land both feet on. The rules are hers. Jump island to island, and whoever lands in the sea goes back to the start. Draw a shark in the gap she finds easiest. It washes off in the first rain, which in this heat means September.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and gets the third sponge. He will not run it anywhere useful; he carries it across the grass, drops it, picks it up and sets off again. His own shallow tray with an inch of water in it goes at the far side, clear of the racing, so the sponge has somewhere to go. Never leave him beside a full bucket while you are timing a round.

second.title: Best Castle, Best Door, Best Moat
second.intro: Three bowls of yesterday's damp sand, three builders, and three prizes named before anybody starts.
materials: The damp sand from Saturday, split between 3 bowls
3 paper flags on craft sticks or straws, plus masking tape to fix them
steps: Three bowls out on the grass, one each, name stone on the rim of each.
Say the three prizes out loud now, before a single handful gets moved: Best Castle, Best Door, Best Moat.
Pitcher on the grass for topping up; sand that dried out overnight needs a splash before it holds.
Build for as long as it runs, twenty minutes or forty. Cups as molds, spoons for digging the moat and cutting the door.
Tear three paper triangles for flags, tape one to a craft stick each, and everyone plants theirs when they are finished.
Judge it out loud and hand out all three prizes. Say what won each one and mean it.
Photograph the three castles side by side with the name stones in front, then let her flatten hers.
second.tip: Build a trash castle yourself. She spends half the time watching what you are doing, and a wonky door gives her room to make hers her own way.

alternatives: One big castle, everybody on it.
Sand in the bowls and no prizes at all.
Build the house you live in out of sand instead.
Press shells, stones and craft sticks into a bowl of flattened sand.
outAgain: The indoor play center, and the cool air is the whole reason
The library, if this is a library week for you
The shaded end of the park with a cold drink each
A friend's house, indoors, with the curtains shut against the sun
The supermarket freezer aisle and one thing she chooses
days.krestonPM: He gets the third bowl of sand and no prize he understands. At 13 months he climbs, so at the play center the low soft steps are where he wants to be rather than the ball pit. Follow him up them. Say happy building to him when the flags go in.

insight.headline: Competition at three works when everyone wins something real.
paras: Azlyn is old enough to want to win and too young to take a loss without the afternoon ending. Three-year-olds have started measuring themselves against other people, which is the reason she ran so hard this morning, and their sense of fairness runs well ahead of their ability to absorb coming second. Naming the three prizes before anyone builds keeps the wanting and takes out the wreckage. She hears three real categories, picks one to aim at, and wins a thing she chose in front of the whole family. Losing well arrives around five or six on its own schedule, and an afternoon where everybody wins something real costs her nothing while she waits.

days.safety: Wet paving and running feet. Run the game on grass where you have it, and on paving everybody walks the course rather than runs it, with the finish buckets standing on a towel. The buckets stay full for the length of one game and get tipped between rounds, because Kreston will head straight for them the second the shouting starts. Sand goes in eyes at the castles, so rinse with clean water and no rubbing. Water into both of them every half hour, hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

days.title: The Beach at Home
days.prepTonight: Tip the three bowls of sand back into the box, then put a paper grocery bag by the back door with the old sheet, the clothespins, the towels and the sun cream.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Windbreak and the Towel Line

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Last Warm Bath of the Beach Week

opening.title: Everything the Week Made
opening.need: 1 laundry basket · the week's pile · her.
steps: Send her round the house with the basket for everything this week made: the fleet, the sea bottle, the name stones, the box of sand, the paintings.
Lay it out on the kitchen floor and let her name each thing and the day it came from. She will get two wrong.
It all goes back in the basket by the back door for 9:15.

main.title: The Windbreak and the Towel Line
materials: 4 dining chairs, or 2 chairs and the clothesline
The 3 paper flags on craft sticks from yesterday
The boats, the sea bottle, the name stones and the box of sand from this week
steps: Sun cream and hats before anything comes out of the basket. Everything after nine happens outdoors.

Two chairs on the grass with their backs together, the other two a body's length away, or one chair at each end of the clothesline. Clip the sheet along the backs with all eight pegs, curved into a corner.
Towels down inside it, edge to edge, until no grass shows. Shoes come off at the edge.
She unpacks the basket: boats in a row, the sea bottle in the sun, a name stone in each corner, the box of sand at one end.
The three flags from yesterday's castles spaced along the top edge of the windbreak.
Sit down in it and do nothing for ten minutes. She built the place; let her be in it first.
main.tip: Clip the sheet so it curves. A flat sheet is a clothesline; a curved one is a room.

outside.title: Beachcombing Without a Beach
paras: Take the paper grocery bag down the shady side of the street and hunt for what a beach has and this garden does not: a smooth stone, a long straight stick for a flagpole, a feather, a dry seed head, a curl of bark. Five things, and each one earns its place by her saying what it would be at the sea. They go into the windbreak at home.

days.infant: Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him the bag to hold between finds and let him drop each one in himself. Anything smaller than his fist goes into your pocket rather than his hand. He will want to sit down on the warm sidewalk, so put the back of your hand on it first.

second.title: Everybody in the Pool
second.intro: The pool goes up on the flattest ground you have and everyone gets in.
materials: 1 paddling pool (substitute: 2 large storage boxes, or the bath)
Warm water, mixed by pitcher from the kettle and the tap
The fleet of boats from Friday
steps: Pool on the flattest, shadiest spot within reach of the tap. Rinse it and let it warm through for twenty minutes.

Fill it cold from the tap. Sit Azlyn and Kreston down on the grass at the far side, and carry the two pitchers of hot water out only once they are both down. Stir them through with your arm and test it with your own elbow.
Now everyone gets in. You first, Kreston on your lap, and Azlyn watches her mother sit in a paddling pool in her clothes.
Pitchers and cups first: pour over shoulders, fill, tip, fill again. The colander held over a head makes rain.
Friday's fleet comes in, all four boats sailing round three people's knees.
Sunday's sea bottle goes in last. She tips it end over end under the surface and watches one wave run the length of it while the whole thing floats.
Lunch on the towels and the afternoon out there. Sun cream again once everyone is dry.
second.tip: Get in. She has spent a week doing water at arm's length in bowls and buckets.

alternatives: Two storage boxes instead of the pool, one foot in each.
The bath, filled shallow, with the fleet and the sea bottle.
Feet in a bowl on the back step and a book each.
outAgain: The post office, and she posts the letter and carries the change
The corner store for a popsicle each, eaten on the wall outside
The library for a stack of sea books to end the week on
Back in the pool, which is where she will vote to go
days.krestonPM: At 13 months he can sit in two inches of warm water and stay busy for five or ten minutes at a stretch, coming back to it across the afternoon, and he will try to stand up every four minutes. Keep a hand on him. He gets a cup of his own, and on the errand he walks the last stretch holding one finger.

insight.headline: Historical injustice, explained plainly, does not damage a three-year-old.
paras: Everyone in your house got in the water today. In America, public pools and beaches were closed to Black families inside living memory, which is why whole generations there were never taught to swim and why the drowning-rate gap still sits where it does. Azlyn reads a hesitation as a rule about what may be said, so say it without the flinch: there was a time when some people were kept out of the water because of their skin, that was wrong, and people changed it. Say it once, answer the follow-up, let her get back in. She may hand it back to you wrong next week. Correct it in one sentence and leave it there.

days.safety: The paddling pool is the real hazard of the week. Kreston is 13 months and walks, so he is within arm's reach every second it holds water and it is never left filled while you go indoors. The kettle stays in the kitchen, and the hot water crosses the garden only while both children are sitting down at the far side. Everything after nine runs outdoors: hat on, cream at nine, cream again at eleven, and once more after the pool.
